title: Urinary incontinence and overactive bladder in women
subject: urology
summary: Classify incontinence as stress, urgency (overactive bladder) or mixed and treat the predominant type: supervised pelvic floor training for at least 3 months for stress or mixed, bladder training for at least 6 weeks for urgency, then an OAB medicine (weighing anticholinergic burden in older women) or a beta-3 agonist, and refer when conservative care fails or red flags are present.

sections.title: Classify and assess
items: Classify at the first assessment: stress (leakage on effort, coughing or sneezing), urgency or overactive bladder (urgency with or without leakage, frequency, nocturia), or mixed; direct initial treatment at the predominant symptom.

Look for contributing factors: UTI, constipation, diuretics and other drugs, diabetes, high fluid or caffeine intake, obesity, reduced mobility, cognitive impairment, genitourinary syndrome of menopause and prolapse.
Bladder diary for at least 3 days covering working and leisure days. Use a validated symptom and quality-of-life questionnaire when evaluating treatment.
Examine the abdomen and pelvis (prolapse, atrophy, masses) and confirm pelvic floor contraction digitally before supervised pelvic floor training.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Urine dipstick in all women for blood, glucose, protein, leucocytes and nitrites.

UTI symptoms with leucocytes and nitrites: send midstream urine culture and treat. No UTI symptoms and both positive: culture, but do not give antibiotics before the result. No symptoms and either negative: do not send culture.
Measure post-void residual by bladder scan if voiding dysfunction or recurrent UTI is suspected.

Do not use pad tests, cystoscopy or imaging in routine assessment. Urodynamics before stress incontinence surgery only if urge-predominant or unclear type, voiding dysfunction, anterior or apical prolapse, or previous continence surgery.

sections.title: First-line conservative treatment
items: Stress or mixed incontinence: supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least 3 months, at least 8 contractions 3 times a day; continue if it helps.
Urgency or mixed incontinence: bladder training for at least 6 weeks; add an OAB medicine if benefit is inadequate and frequency is troublesome.
Lifestyle: a trial of caffeine reduction for OAB; adjust fluid intake if very high or low; weight loss if BMI above 30 kg/m2.
Consider electrical stimulation or biofeedback only for women who cannot actively contract the pelvic floor; do not use it routinely.
Pads and containment products are not treatment: use them only while awaiting treatment, as an adjunct, or long term after options are explored, with review at least yearly.

sections.title: Medicines for overactive bladder
items: Before starting, explain likely benefit, dry mouth and constipation, that full benefit may take 4 weeks, and that long-term effects of anticholinergics on cognition are uncertain.

Offer the anticholinergic with the lowest acquisition cost (for example oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin or trospium); if ineffective or not tolerated, try another; use a transdermal preparation if oral medicines are not tolerated.

Weigh coexisting conditions (poor bladder emptying, cognitive impairment, dementia), total anticholinergic load from other drugs, and cognitive risk. Do not give immediate-release oxybutynin to frail older women at risk of sudden deterioration.
Beta-3 agonists (mirabegron, vibegron) when anticholinergics are unsuitable, ineffective or not tolerated; check BP before and during mirabegron.
Vaginal oestrogen for OAB with genitourinary syndrome of menopause. Systemic HRT does not treat incontinence.
Desmopressin may be considered for troublesome nocturia; avoid it over 65 with cardiovascular disease or hypertension. Do not use flavoxate, propantheline or imipramine.
Duloxetine is not first line for stress incontinence; offer it second line only if she prefers drugs to surgery or is unsuitable for surgery, with counselling on side effects.

sections.title: Review
items: Review 4 weeks after starting or changing an OAB medicine (sooner if side effects are intolerable); change dose or drug if response is poor and review again after 4 weeks.
Long-term OAB medicine: review every 12 months, or every 6 months if over 75.
After at least 3 months of supervised pelvic floor training, reassess symptoms; continue the programme if it helps, otherwise discuss further options.
Offer follow-up within 6 months after stress incontinence surgery (including a vaginal examination after mesh sling surgery).

sections.title: Refer to specialist care
items: Refer if: persistent bladder or urethral pain, palpable bladder after voiding, pelvic mass, faecal incontinence, suspected neurological disease, voiding difficulty, suspected fistula, previous continence or pelvic cancer surgery, or previous pelvic radiotherapy.
Haematuria or recurrent or persistent unexplained UTI: follow the suspected urological cancer pathway.
OAB not responding to medicines: urodynamics, then (after MDT review) bladder botulinum toxin A 100 units if she accepts possible self-catheterisation, or percutaneous sacral nerve stimulation.

Stress incontinence after failed conservative treatment: surgical choice of colposuspension, autologous rectus fascial sling or retropubic mid-urethral mesh sling (a permanent implant); bulking agents if these are unsuitable.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Adding an anticholinergic in an older woman already on other anticholinergic drugs or with cognitive impairment.
Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in incontinent older women.
Missing chronic retention with overflow (palpable bladder, high residual).
Judging an OAB medicine before 4 weeks, or offering pads as the only management.

drugs.name: Solifenacin
drugs.dose: 5 mg orally once daily, increased to 10 mg if needed
drugs.notes: Anticholinergic. Dry mouth, constipation; caution with cognitive impairment and poor bladder emptying.

drugs.name: Oxybutynin (immediate release)
drugs.dose: 5 mg orally two or three times daily (start 2.5 mg twice daily in older women)
drugs.notes: Low cost but most anticholinergic effects; avoid in frail older women. Transdermal patch if oral not tolerated.

drugs.name: Tolterodine
drugs.dose: 2 mg orally twice daily (1 mg twice daily if poorly tolerated or hepatic impairment)

drugs.name: Trospium
drugs.dose: 20 mg orally twice daily before food
drugs.notes: Anticholinergic; reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Mirabegron
drugs.dose: 50 mg orally once daily (25 mg in moderate renal or hepatic impairment)
drugs.notes: Beta-3 agonist without anticholinergic burden. Contraindicated in severe uncontrolled hypertension; monitor BP.

drugs.name: Vaginal oestradiol
drugs.dose: 10 microgram vaginal tablet daily for 2 weeks, then twice weekly
drugs.notes: OAB with genitourinary syndrome of menopause.

drugs.name: Botulinum toxin type A (intravesical)
drugs.dose: 100 units by bladder wall injection; 200 units for later treatments if response is inadequate or short-lived
drugs.notes: Specialist use after MDT review; she must accept possible clean intermittent self-catheterisation.

drugs.name: Duloxetine
drugs.notes: Second line for stress incontinence only. Nausea common; taper when stopping.
